title: Respiratory effect of beta-blocker eye drops in asthma: population-based study and meta-analysis of clinical trials
authors: Morales DR, Dreischulte T, Lipworth BJ, Donnan PT, Jackson C, Guthrie B
population: People with asthma and ocular hypertension in the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink, 2000 to 2012, in a nested case-control study of moderate exacerbations (rescue steroids in primary care) and severe exacerbations (hospitalisation), with a systematic review and meta-analysis of trials of ocular beta-blockers in people with asthma
funder: The role of one author was funded by a Scottish Government Chief Scientist Office Clinical Academic Fellowship (CAF1107). No funding bodies had any role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript.
authorConflicts: One author has received research support, consultancy and lecture fees from Chiesi, Teva, Pharmaxis, Nycomed, Gurnos, Hexal and GlaxoSmithKline; another has received consulting fees from the Scottish Medicines Consortium and grants from GlaxoSmithKline, Otsuka and Amgen.
result: Prescribing of non-selective beta-blocker eye drops to people with asthma and ocular hypertension fell from 23.0% to 13.4% between 2000 and 2012, and of selective ones from 10.5% to 0.9%. Acute exposure to non-selective beta-blocker eye drops raised the relative incidence of moderate asthma exacerbations (incidence rate ratio 4.83, 95% CI 1.56 to 14.94); chronic exposure did not. In the meta-analysis, acute non-selective eye drops lowered FEV1 by a mean 10.9% (-14.9 to -6.9), with falls of 20% or more in one in three; selective eye drops in people sensitive to non-selective ones lowered FEV1 by 6.3% (-11.7 to -0.8).
